analysis.one_liner: Strips federal agencies of authority to regulate greenhouse gases and blocks state climate rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Power Subcommittee but never received a vote before the 112th Congress ended, so EPA's existing greenhouse gas rules stayed in force.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped the President, EPA, and other agencies from regulating carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases for climate reasons. It would have voided EPA's 2009 finding that greenhouse gases endanger public health and every rule built on it, barred future court claims against emitters over climate harm, and stripped states of authority to regulate or tax greenhouse gases, including California's authority to set stricter car emissions standards. Only voluntary programs and existing car rules for 2012-2016 model years would have survived.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal-fired power plants, oil and gas producers, and other large emitters, who would face no federal limits on carbon emissions and could not be sued for their contribution to climate change.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the President and every federal agency from controlling greenhouse gas emissions or considering climate effects unless they first find direct human exposure harm from a concentration far above global levels — a bar that climate-driven rules like EPA's endangerment finding could not meet.
Nullifies EPA's 2009 endangerment finding and the greenhouse gas permitting and reporting rules issued under it, stripping them of all force.
Bars any lawsuit, common-law nuisance claim, or tort liability for a greenhouse gas emitter's contribution to climate change.

Prohibits EPA from granting or honoring Clean Air Act waivers for state greenhouse gas standards for cars from model year 2017 on, and strikes greenhouse gas provisions from state implementation plans, so no state could run its own carbon program.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people, who would bear the health effects of unchecked air pollution and the escalating costs of climate change — stronger storms, crop losses, wildfire, and flood damage — with no federal, state, or court path to limit emissions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone exposed to pollution and climate risk

drawbacks.text: It would void the EPA endangerment finding, the permitting rules built on it, and mandatory emissions reporting, leaving carbon emissions from power plants and industry entirely unregulated at the federal level.

It would strip states — including California — of the ability to set their own greenhouse gas limits for cars and to regulate or tax emissions under state programs, and would make state carbon limits unenforceable.
It would bar private citizens from bringing nuisance or tort claims over climate damage, closing the courthouse as well as the regulator.

A good-faith supporter would acknowledge the bill's stated rationale — that climate policy should be written by Congress rather than inferred from older clean-air statutes — and that the existing car rules from 2012-2016 are preserved; the bill does not repeal those already-issued vehicle standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill preserves one narrow carve-out — the already-final 2010 car standards for 2012-2016 model years — but otherwise removes every tool for limiting greenhouse gases: federal rules, state programs, and civil lawsuits alike. The costs it shields industry from would fall on the public as pollution and climate damage. Even its mechanism for allowing any future federal action — a finding of imminent harm from direct human exposure at concentrations far above global levels — is written so that climate-based regulation could not qualify.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, and it sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg introduced the bill on February 16, 2011, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On February 28, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, and no further action was taken for the rest of the two-year Congress.
The bill drew 104 cosponsors, all of them Republicans, and never advanced past subcommittee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the outcome, but the public kept the protections the bill would have removed: EPA's greenhouse gas rules, state carbon programs, and the right to sue over emissions all remained in force. The fossil fuel interests that would have been the bill's main beneficiaries got nothing beyond its 104 cosponsors.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill never advanced

for.name: Tim Walberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar federal greenhouse gas regulation and state climate rules.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Rep. Fred Upton, R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, never scheduling a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 104 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote where the split could be measured.

industries.industry: Coal-fired power plants and fossil fuel producers
industries.note: The bill would eliminate every federal limit on their carbon emissions, void the rules already applying to them, and shield them from climate-related lawsuits. The compliance costs it removes would reappear as pollution and climate damage borne by the public.

The bill locks the 2010 national greenhouse gas and fuel economy rule for 2012-2016 model years in place 'without further modification or revision', giving automakers regulatory certainty. It would block the stricter California standards that apply to cars from model year 2017 on.

The bill would void the mandatory greenhouse gas emissions reporting rule and bar states from limiting imports of products or electricity based on their carbon content, removing reporting burdens and blocking low-carbon fuel standards like California's.
